titleEn: You turned my mourning into dancing
progression: | Am Am | F G | C Am | E Am |
intro: Thirteen verses of a man reporting his own rescue, said every morning at the opening of the psalms of praise and again through Chanukah. The heading calls it a song for the dedication of a house, and then the body never mentions a house: it is illness, a pit, a hidden face and a recovery. Grammatically it is the best place in the psalter to learn two suffixes at once, the -ta ending that means You did something and the -ni ending that means to me, because almost every verb here carries one or both.

stichs.en: A psalm, a song.
For the dedication of the House. Of David.

verses.summary: The heading names an occasion the poem never returns to. Everything after this line is one man's body and one man's grave, which is why the fit between title and text has been argued over for centuries.

stichs.en: I will exalt You, LORD, for You drew me up,
and did not let my enemies rejoice over me.

verses.summary: The verb for drawing up is the one used of hauling a bucket out of a well, which sets the shaft and the pit that the next verses live in. The reason for praise is given before any of the story is told.

stichs.en: LORD my God, I cried out to You,
and You healed me.

verses.summary: Two words for the whole crisis and its answer. The healing arrives in a single word carrying both the You who acted and the me it acted on.

stichs.en: LORD, You brought my soul up from Sheol,
You kept me alive, from going down to the pit.

verses.summary: The rescue is described as vertical: up out of Sheol, back from the edge of the pit. Whether the speaker was already down there or only heading there depends on how one word is read.

stichs.en: Sing to the LORD, you His faithful ones,
and give thanks to His holy name.

verses.summary: The private report turns outward and becomes an instruction to a congregation. A personal recovery is being handed over as public evidence.

stichs.en: For a moment passes in His anger,
a lifetime in His favour.
At evening weeping lodges for the night,
and at morning, a glad cry.

verses.summary: The proverb at the centre of the psalm, and the tightest line in it: two nouns against two nouns, then night against morning with no verb in the second half at all. Weeping is given the verb for staying overnight, as a guest who leaves.

stichs.en: And I, I said in my ease:
I shall never be shaken.

verses.summary: The flashback begins, and the pronoun is emphatic: and I, for my part. What follows is the sentence that the illness came to answer.

stichs.en: LORD, by Your favour You had set my mountain firm;
You hid Your face,
I was terrified.

verses.summary: Three clauses with nothing joining them, which is the whole point: security, withdrawal, panic, with no connective allowed in between. The security itself is credited to God, so the collapse is not a change of owner but a change of view.

stichs.en: To You, LORD, I call,
and to my Lord I plead for grace.

verses.summary: The verse that opens the quotation: from here to the end of verse eleven the speaker is repeating the prayer he made while sick, not praying it now.

stichs.en: What profit is there in my blood,
in my going down to the grave?
Will dust give You thanks?
Will it declare Your faithfulness?

verses.summary: The argument is commercial before it is theological: a dead worshipper is a loss on both sides. The two questions expect the answer no, and the prefix that marks them as questions is a single letter.

stichs.en: Hear, LORD, and be gracious to me;
LORD, be my helper.

verses.summary: The quoted prayer ends in bare imperatives with no reasons attached. The argument of the previous verse has been made; what is left is the request.

stichs.en: You turned my wailing into dancing for me,
You loosened my sackcloth
and girded me with gladness.

verses.summary: Mourning clothes come off and gladness is put on in their place, worn like a belt. Nothing is undone here; the same material is turned around, which is what the verb means.

stichs.en: so that my glory may sing to You and not be silent.
LORD my God, I will thank You forever.

verses.summary: The rescue is given a purpose, and the purpose is speech. The forever here answers the forever of verse seven: the same word, moved from a boast about stability to a promise of thanks.

pardes.body: The shape is a thanksgiving report. Verses 2 to 6 announce the rescue and call others to join; verses 7 to 11 go back and tell the story, complacency first, then the hidden face, then the prayer quoted word for word; verses 12 and 13 return to the present with the reversal accomplished. The illness is never named and the enemies never act, which keeps the psalm usable by anyone who has been pulled back from something. Watch the two forevers: {{7.5}} is the boast that failed, {{13.7}} is the promise that stands.

Two hard words. In {{4.6}} the consonants can be read as from my going down to the pit or as from among those going down to the pit, and translations still split on it: one has the speaker turned back at the edge, the other has him already down among the dead and hauled out. In {{8.3}} the noun for my mountain carries a prefix that will not sit comfortably in the sentence, so some read You established strength for my mountain and others You established my mountain as a stronghold. Neither reading changes the psalm, but the learner should know the line is rough in Hebrew and smooth only in translation.

The gap between the heading and the poem is where the interpretation happens. The house of {{1.2}} has been read as the Temple that David prepared but did not build, as David's own palace, and as the site bought after the plague at the end of Second Samuel, where a personal deliverance and a future altar occupy the same ground. All three readings are old and none is decisive. Liturgy took the widest option: the psalm is said on Chanukah, treating dedication as rededication, and its daily recitation before the morning psalms lets an individual waking up borrow the vocabulary of a rebuilt sanctuary.

The hiding of the face in {{8.5}} and {{8.6}} became a technical term in later Jewish thought for a concealment that is itself a mode of relation, not an absence. Read that way, verse 6 is not consolation about bad moods but a measurement: anger occupies a moment, favour occupies the duration, and the two are not symmetrical quantities. The turning verb of {{12.0}} is then the key to the whole psalm. Mourning is not deleted and replaced with joy; it is rotated, the same substance seen from the other side, which is why the sackcloth is untied rather than torn off.
